Aethel V1

Polariton-Based Photonic Inference Engine — Technical Analysis & Architecture Comparison
APLD-MPS Simulation Suite v0.4.0  |  Generated: March 2026  |  CONFIDENTIAL DRAFT

1 — Executive Summary

This document presents simulation-derived performance projections for the Aethel V1, a hypothetical room-temperature polariton logic device operating on a monolithic sapphire substrate. All numbers were generated by the APLD-MPS multiphysics simulation suite (Modules B, F, I) and are theoretical upper bounds contingent on hardware that does not yet exist.

22,000 Tokens/s (Llama-3-8B, target)
< 1 mW Power at 22k tok/s
237 GHz Thermo-optic breakdown
Honest framing for readers of this document: The Aethel V1 is a simulation-only architecture. No physical prototype exists. The comparison to NVIDIA B200 contrasts a hypothetical photonic system against shipping silicon. The gap between simulation and reality is addressed in Section 5.

Why the efficiency gap is so large: Electronic transistors dissipate ~1 pJ per switching event due to capacitive charging of metal interconnects. Polariton gates operate via photon interference in a dielectric medium, theoretically avoiding resistive losses entirely. The 0.5 aJ figure is the simulation's assumed switching energy and sits ~2,000× above the Landauer limit (kBT·ln2 ≈ 2.87 × 10-21 J at 300 K). This is plausible physics but unverified in hardware.

Why 22,000 tok/s and not 60 billion? The 22,000 tok/s target is a conservative engineering target chosen for first-generation hardware. It accounts for: (a) imperfect gate fabrication reducing yield, (b) control-plane overhead for weight loading, (c) error-correction cycles, and (d) I/O bandwidth limits at the fiber-to-chip interface. The simulation's theoretical peak (110M tok/s single-pipeline, or ~60B at 1 kW) represents the physical ceiling of the architecture, not a deliverable spec.

4 — Thermal Stability & Breakdown Analysis

4.1 — The Thermo-Optic Feedback Problem

Every irreversible logic operation dissipates at least kBT·ln2 ≈ 2.87 zJ of heat (Landauer principle). At high clock rates, cumulative heating shifts the sapphire refractive index via the thermo-optic effect (dn/dT = 1.3 × 10-5 K-1), which degrades the interference contrast of MZI-based logic gates.

Feedback loop: f_clk ↑ → P_diss ↑ → ΔT ↑ → Δn = (dn/dT) · ΔT → Δφ = (2π/λ) · Δn · L → ER ↓

Our CoupledThermoFDTDSimulator implements this as a runtime feedback loop: the FDTD solver's permittivity map εr(r) is updated every 50 EM steps with the thermal correction Δεr = 2n·Δn from the spectral heat diffusion solver.

What this means in practice: At the 22,000 tok/s target, the effective clock rate is far below 1 GHz. The thermal headroom is enormous — the breakdown limit of 237 GHz would support ~110 million tokens/s. Thermal stability is not the bottleneck for this architecture.

5 — Critical Risk Factor: Holographic SCO Memory

Every architecture comparison in this document rests on the assumption that the Aethel V1 can store and retrieve neural network weights at photonic speeds. This capability depends on a memory technology that does not yet exist: holographic readout of spin-crossover (SCO) molecular arrays. We detail this risk because we believe intellectual honesty is the most credible foundation for any technical pitch.

5.1 — What the Simulation Assumes

Memory parameterAssumed valueExperimental status
Cell pitch 50 nm Undemonstrated. Smallest SCO single-molecule devices: ~100 nm (academic)
Read mechanism Holographic recall, 0.1 ps No published demonstration of holographic SCO readout
Write (switch) time 0.5 ps Partial. Ultrafast spin-crossover switching observed in fs pump-probe studies
Read energy 1 fJ per cell Estimated; no direct measurement available
Retention time 106 μs (~17 min) Plausible for thermally bistable SCO; depends on ligand engineering
Capacity needed (Llama-3-8B) 5.56 GB (INT8) Requires ~4.4 × 1010 individually addressable SCO cells

5.2 — Technology Readiness Assessment

Critical — Holographic SCO Memory
TRL 1-2 (Basic principles observed, no lab prototype)

No published work demonstrates holographic addressing of SCO molecular arrays. The simulation models readout as a single 0.1 ps timing constant with no diffraction physics, no crosstalk model, and no error rate. This is the single largest uncertainty in the entire architecture.

Moderate — Polariton Logic Gates
TRL 3-4 (Lab demonstrations exist)

All-optical switching using exciton-polaritons has been demonstrated in multiple labs at room temperature (e.g., WS2 cavities, perovskite microcavities). Integration into logic circuits is unproven at scale.

Low — Sapphire Substrate
TRL 8-9 (Mature industrial product)

Sapphire wafers up to 300 mm diameter are routinely manufactured for LED and semiconductor applications. Thermal and optical properties are well-characterized.

Moderate — TMD Monolayer Integration
TRL 3-4 (Lab-scale CVD growth demonstrated)

Wafer-scale WS2 and WSe2 monolayers have been grown on sapphire via MOCVD. Uniformity and defect density for logic applications remain active research areas.

5.3 — What the Simulation Does NOT Model

  • Holographic diffraction patterns and beam fidelity at 50 nm resolution
  • SCO molecular switching statistics (bit-error rate under repeated cycling)
  • Thermal crosstalk between adjacent memory cells
  • Fabrication yield of 44 billion addressable cells per memory region
  • The addressing scheme (how to select one weight among billions)
  • Error correction for holographic readout (no ECC model exists)
Bottom line for investors: If the SCO memory problem is solved, the energy-efficiency advantage is real and physics-based (photonic switching vs. capacitive charging). If SCO memory proves infeasible, the architecture would need an alternative memory technology (e.g., phase-change photonic memory, electro-optic SRAM), which would likely reduce the efficiency advantage by 10-100× but could still outperform electronic inference.

7.2 — TPV Energy Recycling (Module F)

The Aethel-Kreislauf (Aethel cycle) captures waste heat as mid-IR radiation and converts it back to electricity using InGaAsSb thermophotovoltaic cells (Egap = 0.55 eV).

P_rad = ε · σ · A · (T_chip^4 - T_amb^4) η_TPV = 0.4 × η_Carnot × f_above_gap × η_quantum Closed loop: Computation → Heat → IR photons → TPV cell → Electricity → Laser emitters

At the 22,000 tok/s target, power dissipation is 0.37 mW — far too low for meaningful TPV recovery. The TPV system becomes relevant only above ~100 GHz clock rates, where dissipation reaches tens of watts and chip temperature exceeds 320 K.

9 — Conclusion & Roadmap

What the simulation proves

  • The physics is self-consistent. Maxwell's equations (FDTD), the Gross-Pitaevskii equation (polariton dynamics), coupled heat diffusion, and the thermo-optic feedback loop all produce stable, convergent results when run together.
  • The energy advantage is fundamental. Photonic interference consumes ~2,000× less energy per switching event than capacitive electronic switching. This is not an engineering trick but a consequence of the underlying physics.
  • Thermal stability has massive headroom. The breakdown clock rate (237 GHz) is orders of magnitude above the operating point needed for 22,000 tok/s.

What the simulation does NOT prove

  • That the SCO memory can be built. This is the single point of failure. No holographic SCO readout has been demonstrated. Without it, the architecture cannot load weights at photonic speeds.
  • That 201 million polariton gates can be fabricated on one substrate. The largest demonstrated polariton circuits contain < 100 elements.
  • That the interference contrast survives fabrication imperfections. The simulation assumes perfect waveguide geometry. Real devices will have roughness, defects, and strain-induced index variations.
